title: Autocomplete & Typeahead
summary: Serving ranked suggestions within a tight latency budget as the user types — tries, precomputation, and the trade-offs unique to a per-keystroke query.

slides.markdown:
**Autocomplete** (or typeahead) suggests completions as a user types, before they've finished the query — think Google's dropdown after typing "how to fi." It's a different problem from full-text search: the query is a prefix, not a whole phrase, and it fires on *every keystroke*, so the latency budget is far tighter than a normal search request.

This topic covers the data structure that makes prefix matching fast (the trie) and the precomputation tricks that keep a per-keystroke feature from melting your servers.

slides.sectionTitle: What autocomplete optimizes for: latency over completeness
slides.markdown:
A normal search query fires once, after the user commits to it, and users tolerate a couple hundred milliseconds. Autocomplete fires on **every keystroke** — type a 10-character query and you've triggered 10 separate lookups — so it needs to respond in well under 50ms or the UI visibly lags behind typing.

That tight budget means autocomplete deliberately trades completeness for speed: it doesn't need to search entire documents or compute a full relevance score, it just needs the best handful of completions for a prefix, fast. This is why autocomplete uses different underlying machinery (tries, precomputed top-k lists) than the [inverted index](inverted-index) behind full search.

A **trie** (prefix tree) stores strings letter by letter along shared paths: every word starting with "cat" walks through the same `c → a → t` nodes before branching for the rest of the word ("cat," "catalog," "caterpillar"). Looking up all completions for a prefix means walking to the node for that prefix, then collecting every word reachable below it — a single traversal, not a scan of every possible word.

This structure is a natural fit because a user's prefix *is* a trie path: as they type each letter, you're just walking one node deeper, which is exactly why tries are the classic textbook answer to "design typeahead."

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a trie returning top-k completions for a prefix
slides.markdown:
![Trie for prefix "cat" with frequency-ranked completions](assets/trie-autocomplete.svg)

Walking down to the node for "cat" takes just as many steps as the prefix is long — three steps for a three-letter prefix, regardless of how many total words the trie holds. From that node, every word below it is a valid completion; ranking them (usually by frequency or recency) picks which few actually get shown.

The expensive part in practice isn't finding the completions — it's picking the *best* few out of potentially thousands hanging below a common prefix like "a" or "the."

assets.alt: Trie for prefix "cat" with frequency-ranked completions

slides.markdown:
Which completions to show is its own ranking problem, layered on top of the trie lookup. **Frequency** — how often other users have searched this completion; "weather" beats "weathervane" as a completion for "weath" because far more people search the former. **Personalization** — a user's own search history can bump a completion they've searched before, even if it's globally less common. **Recency** — trending or newly popular queries (a breaking news term) can be boosted temporarily above their historical frequency would suggest.

Most production systems blend all three, similar in spirit to the boosting signals covered for full search ranking — global frequency as the base, adjusted up for personal and recency signals.

slides.sectionTitle: Precomputing top-k per prefix to hit tight latency budgets
slides.markdown:
Ranking every completion below a trie node on every keystroke is too slow at scale — a popular one-letter prefix can have millions of matches. The standard fix is to **precompute** and cache the top-k completions for every prefix likely to be queried, ahead of time, usually as a batch job over recent query logs.

At request time, the server does no ranking at all — it just looks up the prefix's precomputed list and returns it, turning an expensive per-request computation into a cheap cache read. The trade-off is staleness: precomputed lists only update on the next batch run, so truly brand-new trending queries lag behind until the next refresh (mitigated by running the batch job frequently, or layering in a small real-time boost for rapidly trending terms).

| | Trie-based | Index-based (search-as-you-type) |
|---|---|---|
| Matches | Prefix of a single term/phrase | Any word anywhere in a multi-word field |
| Example | "cat" completes to "catalog" | "blue shoes" matches "comfortable blue running shoes" |
| Structure | Prefix tree, walked per keystroke | Edge n-grams or a specialized analyzer in an inverted index |
| Ranking | Precomputed top-k by frequency | Standard relevance scoring (BM25-style) applies |
| Best for | Single field, prefix-only suggestions (search box, usernames) | Multi-word product/document titles where the match isn't always a prefix |

**How to decide:** a trie is simpler and faster when completions are genuinely prefix-based (a name, a single search term). Reach for an index-based approach when users expect a match anywhere in a longer phrase, not just at the start.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: recomputing suggestions from scratch on every keystroke
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Just run the ranking query live on every keystroke — it's the same logic either way."

**Why it's wrong:** ranking every completion below a prefix in real time means, for a popular short prefix, scoring potentially millions of candidates — on every single keystroke of every user typing. That's an enormous, avoidable amount of repeated work: the ranked list for "cat" barely changes between one user's request and the next.

**Correct model:** precompute and cache the top-k completions per prefix ahead of time (§ precomputing top-k), so the live request path is a cache lookup, not a ranking computation. Accept a small amount of staleness — refreshed by a frequent batch job — in exchange for a latency budget that live ranking simply cannot hit at scale.

slides.sectionTitle: What a plain trie misses: typos, and why fuzzy prefix matching needs a different structure
slides.markdown:
A pure trie only matches an exact prefix — type "resturant" (missing an 'a') and a trie walking `r-e-s-t-u-r-a-n-t` falls off the tree entirely, returning nothing, even though "restaurant" is an obvious intended match. Typeahead in production has to tolerate at least one or two edit-distance errors, which a plain character-by-character trie walk can't do on its own.

The standard fix layers a **Levenshtein automaton** (or a precomputed edit-distance-bounded index) on top of the trie: instead of walking one exact path, the search explores every trie path within edit distance k of the typed prefix simultaneously, pruning branches that can't possibly stay within budget. This is more expensive per keystroke than an exact walk, which is why production systems often cap it to edit distance 1-2 and apply it only once the typed prefix is at least 3-4 characters, when the number of plausible near-matches is small enough to explore cheaply.

This is the detail that separates a toy trie demo from a typeahead that survives real user typing.
